audit.method: Iterative language-model judgment: compare missing everyday uses with less conversational retained entries; not measured corpus frequency.
scope: noun number, oblique and case forms
verb tense/aspect/agreement and common stem operations
negation, ability, necessity, permission and learned skill
relative, conditional, concessive and temporal constructions
quotatives, focus, questions, indefinites, reports and address
postpositions, comparisons, counters, distribution and connective helper words
audit.stopping_rule: An initial judgment audit was completed, then new passages exposed additional variants and uses. Versions 1.3 through 1.6 include those follow-up examples; coverage is revisable and is not claimed to be exhaustive. Version 1.7 incorporates additional temporal, purpose/manner, positional and stem variants. Version 1.8 follows a further common-use gap review; no exhaustive-coverage claim. Version 1.9 checks patterns in the official Avant Telugu learner response. Version 1.10 extends three existing families with practice-passage examples.

title: Telugu modifier examples and exact Unicode transformations
scope_notes: Version 1.10 adds three practice-passage examples within existing families: కొను → కొన్నాక, పెట్టు → పెట్టాను, కావాలి → కావాల్సింది. The last is explicitly contracted and illustrates past need rather than necessarily unfulfilled duty.

Version 1.9 adds eleven examples from a review of the official Avant Telugu learner-response patterns: వలన, వీటి, వీటితో, habitual/ongoing auxiliary agreement, expanded/contracted cessation-completive, reflexive-progressive and reflexive-modal combinations, nominal dative stem change, and adjective + negative copula. Existing learning families are extended; learner errors are not promoted to new forms.

Version 1.8 adds 24 common-use examples, including inferred anterior విని ఉంటావు/విని ఉంటాడు, anterior conditionals, embedded negatives, prohibitive కూడదు, desire, prospective బోతున్న, past obligation, negative-before, cessation/inception, ఇంకా/మళ్లీ/కలిసి, liking and explicit inflection combinations. Coverage prioritization is language-model judgment, not measured corpus frequency.

Version 1.7 adds eleven passage-follow-up examples: వచ్చినాక, వచ్చాక, ఉన్నాక; relative + లా in తగిలేలా, దొర్లేలా, ఎగిరేలా; positional పై/క్రింద; and తిన్నాను, వేశాను, తీసుకుని. Two new learning families; existing examples and practice progress preserved.

Version 1.6 adds nine examples from the work-from-home passage: abstract త, సరిపడా, negative-emphasis అసలు, paired కీ ... కీ, matching ఎంత ... అంతే, మారుతుంటుంది, చేయాల్సిన, ఉండవచ్చని, and గంటలైనా. Three new learning families cover the two standalone modifiers and the degree-correlative construction; the other examples extend existing families.
Version 1.5 adds ఒకే → ఒకేలా, చేయాలి → చేయాలో, and తీసుకొను → తీసుకుంటాను as variants/combinations within existing entries.
Version 1.4 adds ప్రదేశాలు → ప్రదేశాలన్నీ and ఇద్దరు → ఇద్దరం as examples of totality and first-person counted groups within existing entries.
Version 1.3 adds eight stepwise examples covering టం/టానికి, కో, కుంటూ, తర్వాత, and ఇప్పటికీ from the new passage. These extend existing families; combinations are not new atomic modifiers.
Version 1.2 completes a practical judgment-based audit of common grammatical functions; see audit metadata. This is not a frequency-ranked or exhaustive inventory of Telugu.

Version 1.1 adds common practice forms beyond the original corpus. These are curated for practical coverage, not statistically frequency-ranked. New contexts are constructed examples. Formal passive is explicitly marked.
This is a corpus-based learning inventory, not a count of atomic Telugu morphemes or an exhaustive grammar. Composite constructions are labeled, not expanded into all possible combinations.
Base means the input to THIS step. It can be a dictionary form, oblique stem, relative form, already-inflected form, or bound stem. Bound stems are explicitly noted.

Unicode operations are exact for each example, not rules to apply to every Telugu word. The operation uses the longest common codepoint prefix; its boundary can lie inside a written cluster. This is an encoding diff, not a claimed morpheme boundary.

Modifier_surface identifies the relevant ending/function word. operation additionally captures stem changes and sandhi. Zero operations have null modifier_surface, not a fictional Unicode for the empty string.

Examples are drawn from the supplied material or constructed from its bases. source_context is a locating cue, not a claim that the result always appears as a standalone token. Derived and truncated examples are marked.

The new sample contains spelling errors. These are not new morphological forms: చేస్తుది → చేస్తుంది; ఆలోచలని → ఆలోచనలను; తెలియాదు → తెలియదు; అన్ని → అని in the reporting construction. మరుస్తది is interpreted as మారుస్తుంది based on the supplied corrected word. బైట is represented by supplied బయట.

New material adds negative nonpast తెలియదు, necessitative చేయాల్సి, joined చేయాలంటే, demonstrative ఇలాంటి, and embedded alternative లేదో; existing plural/locative, possibility, object, quotative and question patterns gain examples.
చేయాల్సి is preserved as supplied. The uncontracted form is చేయవలసి. చేయాల్సి వస్తే is a combination: necessitative form + conditional వస్తే, meaning if one has to do it.

Earlier independent negative అక and raw past/nonpast marker rows are represented through contextual constructions/stems rather than inventing free-standing forms. Similar Unicode strings can perform different grammatical functions.

Open-ended lexical adverbs and nouns are not exhaustively inventoried. Common counter constructions such as సారి/సార్లు and మంది are included for practice and labeled as counters, not inflectional suffixes.

Combination notes: లోని = లో + attributive ని; లోకి = లో + కి; manner బాగానే = బాగా + నే; temporal రాగానే is a different construction; కుండానే = కుండా + నే; తున్న = తూ + ఉండు with contraction; ఉన్నట్లుగా = ఉన్న + ట్లు + గా; చేయడానికి includes verbal-noun oblique + కి; ఆడినప్పుడు = ఆడిన + అప్పుడు; చేయాలంటే = చేయాలి + అంటే with sandhi.
Long vowels can express focus, inclusion, or interrogative meaning, depending on the construction. Unicode identity alone does not determine grammar.
